Based on the review of requested and planned content, the teams must reach a consensus on which items to include in the Spell. In some cases, the Spell Crafter may request the removal of certain items if the Spell is deemed high risk, too big or contains novel code. Such removals typically affect non-critical items, such as internal payments. Onboarding of sensitive modules is considered increasing the Spell's complexity in such a manner that the Spell Reviewers should only focus on this; therefore, non-crucial items should be removed from the Executive Sheet and included in the Executive Vote queue.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Final Inclusion Decision
assessments.description: Defines the dispute resolution and decision-making process for including items in a security Spell.
assessments.quote:
Where consensus cannot be reached on whether to include an item in the Spell, the disagreement must be raised in the govops channel in Slack so that the Spell Teams, Core GovOps, the Core Facilitator, and the Protocol Security Workstream Lead have visibility into the disagreement and the reasoning behind it. The Core Facilitator must hear all positions and make the final decision on whether to include the item. The Core Facilitator's decision is binding for the Executive Vote in question.

Routine coordination among the Spell Teams in their own working channels is expected. A disagreement over whether to include an item must not, however, be resolved in a way that excludes the Core Facilitator or that settles the matter privately and reports only the outcome. The positions of each party, and the reasoning through which the disagreement is resolved, must be visible in the govops channel in Slack.

Where a security or confidentiality concern makes it necessary to discuss such a disagreement in a private channel, the parties to that discussion must afterwards provide a substantive accounting in the govops channel in Slack, setting out the positions of each party and how the settled position was reached.

Where there is credible suspicion that the Core Facilitator is compromised, Core GovOps makes the final inclusion decision for the Executive Vote in question in the Core Facilitator's place, and the adjudication process specified in [A.1.7.6 - Acting Against Misalignment](7aafa61e-8649-41fb-8c3f-64e5714f9f18) applies.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule defines a concrete process with named actors (Spell Teams, Core GovOps, Core Facilitator, Protocol Security Workstream Lead) and specific steps (raise in govops channel, Core Facilitator hears all positions and makes binding decision), but it contains no quantitative thresholds, formulas, or metrics; it is a qualitative procedural rule.

assessments.title: Provenance
assessments.description: Mandates sufficient provenance for Executive Sheet actions and prohibits inclusion of items with insufficient provenance in votes.
assessments.quote:
All actions in the Executive Sheet require sufficient provenance for their inclusion in the sheet and later in the Executive Vote. The legitimacy of a provenance is assessed on the basis of its mutability, visibility and resistance to compromise by external malicious actors. There are different ways of providing sufficient provenance, including "strong comment type" provenance, "onchain" provenance and "strong document type" provenance. These types of provenance are defined in the subdocuments herein.

If Executive actions and items do not have sufficient provenance, for example, "weak comment type", they cannot be included in the Executive Vote. If the Governance Point has any question whether a proposed Executive action has sufficient provenance, they must resolve that question of validity before including that action in the Executive Process.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states a real obligation (sufficient provenance required) and names criteria (mutability, visibility, resistance to compromise) and provenance types, but all criteria are qualitative with no numeric thresholds, formulas, or verifiable metrics. Compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule prohibits inclusion of actions lacking sufficient provenance, but enforcement relies on the Governance Point's self-policing. No specific penalty, on-chain mechanism, or named enforcer distinct from the actor is cited; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop would apply, which is weak.

assessments.title: Weak Comment Type Provenance
assessments.description: Prohibits the use of informal or mutable communication channels for authorizing Executive actions.
assessments.quote: The provenance type "weak comment type provenance" refers to informal or editable comments made by stakeholders, which lack the security and visibility needed for Executive actions. For example, Discord messages, forum posts, or unverified social media comments are considered weak comment provenance, even if they relate to an action affecting the commenter (e.g., confirming a payment). Weak comment types are highly mutable, as they can often be edited or deleted without a public trace, and may not be visible to all ecosystem participants (e.g., requiring platform-specific accounts or access to private channels). They also have low resistance to compromise, relying on accounts without strong security protocols, making them vulnerable to malicious edits or takeovers by bad actors. As such, weak comment provenance does not qualify as sufficient and must not be used to authorize Executive actions.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule defines a clear prohibition against using weak comment provenance for Executive actions, with examples and characteristics, but it lacks any quantifiable metric, threshold, or deadline. Compliance is verifiable in principle (a Discord message would be a violation), but the definition relies on qualitative criteria (mutable, low security) leaving edge cases arguable.

In cases where the issue may be non-technical in nature - such as possible instances of collusion - supporting evidence should be captured, which supports the argument that a non-technical issue may be present. This evidence should be captured in a manner that does not permit bad actors to manipulate or erase the evidence through methods such as editing or deleting messages.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule requires documentation and evidence capture but provides no quantifiable metrics, deadlines, or verifiable standards. Phrases like 'investigate the impacts', 'determine how the issue arose', and 'documenting how the issue manifests' are qualitative, and 'capture evidence in a manner that does not permit... manipulation' is vague. A party could argue compliance based on any reasonable effort.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific consequence is defined for failure to prepare documentation. No on-chain mechanism, capital at risk, or named institutional path reaches this rule. Only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop (Reports of Misalignment, Adjudication Process) would apply, which alone is always weak.

assessments.title: Determining the Handling Party
assessments.description: Defines the process for designating a handling party to resolve classified technical issues.
assessments.quote: Once a technical issue has been classified and evidence supporting its existence is collected, an entity needs to be designated as the handling party for resolving the issue. This party will typically be the Core Facilitator. However, if there is a non-trivial chance that the Core Facilitator will ignore or downplay the issue, another entity should serve as the handling party.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states an obligation to designate a handling party but relies entirely on the qualitative judgment 'non-trivial chance' with no quantified threshold, no metrics, and no deadline; compliance is therefore arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific consequence attaches; only the generic misalignment/adjudication catch-all could theoretically apply, which alone is always weak, and no other named mechanism reaches this internal process rule.

assessments.title: Publicly Reporting the Issue
assessments.description: Mandates public reporting of discovered issues unless disclosure poses a security threat to the protocol.
assessments.quote: Discovered issues must be reported publicly unless doing so poses a threat to the security of the Sky Protocol. Technical issues that are currently or likely to become, actively exploitable must not be discussed in a public manner, as this poses a threat to the security of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule creates a clear obligation (report publicly unless actively exploitable) but the trigger condition ('currently or likely to become actively exploitable') is qualitative and open to interpretation; no numeric threshold, metric, or verification method is provided.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism in the catalog applies to this operational reporting rule; consequences would only flow through the catch-all misalignment process, which is weak.

assessments.title: Resolving the Issue and Following Up
assessments.description: Defines the process for addressing and following up on technical issues or protocol threats.
assessments.quote: The Crafter or Reviewer, if they discovered the technical issue, should address or remedy the issue as necessary to resolve it. The handling party (typically the Core Facilitator) must follow up to ensure that the technical issue has been resolved. If the issue poses a threat to the Sky Protocol - such as an exploit or instance of collusion - it should be followed up on as a matter of urgency by the handling party.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule describes obligations qualitatively: 'should address or remedy', 'must follow up', 'should be followed up on as a matter of urgency', with no quantifiable thresholds, deadlines, or verifiable criteria; a third party could not objectively check compliance from the text alone.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism reaches this rule; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop applies, which is weak. No automatic consequences or named enforcer with defined penalties are tied to failing to follow up on technical issues.

assessments.title: Issue Retrospective
assessments.description: Requires documentation of technical issue causes and preventative measures following a resolution.
assessments.quote: Following the resolution of a technical issue, the parties involved in the development process, or other relevant processes leading to the issue arising, must document how the issue arose. These parties (often the Crafter or Reviewer) should also detail any measures that were previously in place to prevent this type of issue occurring, and any measures that can be implemented going forward in order to prevent the same issue from occurring again in the future.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes a qualitative documentation obligation (document how the issue arose, detail past and future measures) but provides no deadlines, format standards, acceptance criteria, or verifiable metrics. Compliance is entirely subjective and arguable.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism is specified or implicitly reaches this documentation requirement. Only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop would apply, which is always weak.

assessments.title: Security First
assessments.description: Mandates that security and safety must be prioritized over efficiency, gas costs, or process speed in all designs.
assessments.quote: Any choice between efficiency and security must always be made to maximize security, even at the cost of time, process inefficiency, or gas cost. Smart contract system designs as well as individual smart contracts, their code, and their interactions must always prioritize increased security over increased efficiency, reduced gas cost, or any other benefits. Rules and processes must always maximize security and safety, even at the cost of inefficiency, repetitiveness, longer review or audit timelines, or other drawbacks.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states a qualitative obligation to 'maximize security' and 'prioritize increased security' over efficiency, gas costs, and process speed, but provides no numeric thresholds, metrics, or objectively verifiable criteria; compliance is entirely a matter of subjective judgment.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism targets this abstract design principle; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstops (A.1.3.2.4, A.1.5.9) are available, which are always weak.

assessments.title: Minimizing Complexity
assessments.description: Mandates prioritizing simple smart contract designs unless complexity provides a significant net increase to protocol security.
assessments.quote: Smart contract system designs, as well as individual smart contracts, their code, and their interactions must always use a simpler design over a more complex design, unless the more complex design provides a significant net increase to the safety and security of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes an obligation to prefer simpler designs, with an exception for a 'significant net increase to safety and security'. No metrics, thresholds, or objective criteria define 'simpler', 'more complex', or 'significant net increase', making compliance a matter of judgment.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism reaches this rule; only the generic misalignment backstop applies. No on-chain enforcement, capital at risk, or named review process is explicitly linked.

assessments.title: Chesterton’s Fence
assessments.description: Requires proponents to explain the historical context and reasoning behind current states before proposing protocol changes.
assessments.quote: Chesterton’s Fence is a principle that states that changes must not be made to the current state of affairs unless the reasoning behind the current state of affairs is understood and can be explained. Changes to the Sky Protocol must only be proposed after the context - such as the reasoning, actions, and history - leading to the thing’s current state are known and can be explained by the party proposing the change. Changes must not be approved by team members or otherwise accepted until all parties responsible for overseeing, checking, or reviewing the change are aware of the context behind the current state of affairs as it exists before the change is enacted.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes a qualitative obligation to understand and explain historical context before proposing or approving changes. It provides no metrics, thresholds, or verifiable conditions; compliance hinges entirely on subjective judgment of whether context is understood and explained, making it arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule is a procedural requirement for proposal and approval, but it relies solely on the actors themselves (proposers, reviewers) to comply. No on‑chain enforcement, capital‑at‑risk, or named escalation path applies, and only the generic catch‑all misalignment process could theoretically be invoked, which is insufficient for a higher rating.

assessments.title: Existing Process Adherence
assessments.description: Mandates compliance with existing processes and requires communication of deviations to the Core Facilitator.
assessments.quote: All existing Sky processes and patterns, whether pertaining to rules, processes, systems, smart contracts, or code, must be complied with. If regular operation is impossible due to a technical limitation or otherwise, it is permitted so long as it does not compromise the safety or security of the Sky Protocol in any way. New patterns developed in this way must prioritize the safety and security of the Sky Protocol over all other considerations and should be as similar to old patterns as possible. However, deviation from industry norms and best practices is encouraged so long as they are made in the interest of maximizing security. Any deviations by the Crafter or Reviewers must be communicated to the Core Facilitator.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes a real obligation to comply with existing processes and communicate deviations, but all criteria are qualitative (e.g., 'do not compromise safety', 'as similar as possible', 'prioritize safety'). No thresholds, metrics, deadlines, or verifiable conditions are provided; compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism explicitly reaches this process adherence rule. The communication requirement to the Core Facilitator is not backed by any stated consequence, and the general misalignment adjudication alone is always weak.

assessments.title: Tenth Man Mandate
assessments.description: Mandates a contrarian reviewer to attempt to disprove unanimous governance decisions before implementation.
assessments.quote: If a group of people making a decision unanimously holds a certain opinion, all make the same assumption or all come to the same conclusion, it is the responsibility of one member of the group to assume that the rest of the group is incorrect. The member of the group assigned to hold this contrarian viewpoint is referred to as the ‘tenth man’ and must attempt to disprove the group’s decision. Where the ‘tenth man’ is able to provide compelling arguments against the group’s conclusion, the decision must be reassessed.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes a qualitative obligation (assign a 'tenth man' to attempt to disprove a unanimous decision and reassess if 'compelling arguments' are provided) but provides no numeric thresholds, measurable criteria, or defined cadence; compliance is purely judgment-based and arguable.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism targets this internal governance process rule; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop applies.

assessments.title: Providing Voters With Sufficient Information
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to provide documentation and summaries to voters for informed decision-making.
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that voters have access to sufficient information to make informed decisions. This might include:

- Links to documentation or discussions related to the actions included in the Executive Document.
- Summaries of the actions included in the Executive Document, created by unbiased and knowledgeable third parties.
- Links to any analysis published by DAO-funded entities regarding the actions in the Executive Document.
- Links to well-maintained resources describing the nature of any parameters that may be changed if the Executive Proposal passes.

Providing accessible and complete information is essential to maintaining the legitimacy of the process. Voters should not later regret their vote due to a lack of understanding of the actions they voted on.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to 'ensure voters have access to sufficient information' is expressed in judgment language; the 'might include' items are non-exhaustive examples with no numeric thresholds, metrics, deadlines, or verifiable criteria. Compliance depends entirely on qualitative assessment.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism applies to this information-provision duty; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop (catch-all) could theoretically reach a violation, which is weak.

assessments.title: Ensuring Transparency And Clarity
assessments.description: Mandates that the Core Facilitator provides clear, transparent, and detailed information within Executive Documents for voters.
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that the Executive Document is clear, transparent, and accessible to all voters. This involves eliminating ambiguity and confusion to the greatest extent possible while balancing technical detail with readability. Voters should clearly understand:

- The effects and impacts of the Executive Vote if passed.
- The processes that led to each item being included in the Executive Document.
- The identities (pseudonymous or entity-level) of those responsible for publishing, writing, and reviewing the Executive Vote.

The goal is to ensure that voters are always provided with information on why an item is included, what will happen if the Executive Vote passes, or who is responsible for its contents.

Clarity reduces the risk of disruption, confusion, or a breakdown of legitimacy in the governance process.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes a real obligation on the Core Facilitator to make Executive Documents clear, transparent, and accessible, and lists categories of information voters should understand, but all criteria are expressed in qualitative judgment language without any numeric thresholds, metrics, deadlines, or verifiable conditions. Compliance could be plausibly argued either way on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism is cited or implied for this qualitative duty. Only the generic misalignment and adjudication catch-all processes (A.1.3.2.4, A.1.5.9) would apply, which are always weak. There is no on-chain, capital-at-risk, or institutional penalty path linked to this rule.

assessments.title: Balancing Technical Detail And Accessibility
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to balance technical detail and readability in Executive Documents for voters.
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that the Executive Document balances technical detail with readability. Voters should not require in-depth technical knowledge of the Sky Protocol to understand the Executive Document.
Guidelines for Technical Detail:

- Avoid including excessive technical details that obscure clarity or clutter the Executive Document.
- Include technical details only when they are strictly necessary, such as:
    - In emergency or urgent responses when technical details are the primary focus of the proposal.
    - For non-urgent technical fixes or housekeeping when technical details are relevant, but should be given lower priority compared to other actions in the Executive Vote.

In cases where technical details are included, the Governance Point must ensure they fully understand the technical aspects themselves to present them accurately and clearly.

Excessive technical detail can overwhelm voters and obscure the document's primary purpose. By carefully managing technical content, the Core Facilitator ensures that the document remains accessible and focused.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule is entirely qualitative: 'balances technical detail with readability,' 'avoid including excessive technical details,' 'include only when strictly necessary' are all judgment calls with no measurable thresholds, cadence, or objectively verifiable criteria. A third party could not determine compliance from the text alone, making it arguable either way.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism addresses this obligation; only the general misalignment/adjudication backstop exists, which alone is always weak. Artifact review (d4bf73e7) might plausibly cover document quality, but the rule's focus on readability is not tied to any defined review criteria or consequences.

assessments.title: Executive Summary
assessments.description: Defines mandatory parameters for Executive Summaries including GSM pause delays, office-hours modifiers, and 90-day spell expiration limits.
assessments.quote:
The Executive Summary outlines the key actions that will occur if the proposal passes. It includes:

- The GSM Pause Delay, which specifies the minimum time before the Spell can be executed and is enforced by ds-pause.
- The Office-Hours Modifier, if applicable, which restricts execution to specific times.
- The Expiration Date of the Spell.
    - The Spell must always have an expiration date; it can’t be more than 90 days in the future, and the typical expiration window is 30 days.
- A high-level explanation of the actions being performed in the Spell, presented in bullet-point form.

The summary should provide a high-level overview of the Executive Vote and ensure that SKY holders can quickly understand the scope and purpose of the proposal. This section also explains that voting for the proposal with SKY places support for these actions.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states a concrete numeric limit: the Spell's expiration date must exist and may not be more than 90 days in the future. This is objectively verifiable, though the exact reference point for 'in the future' is not defined, leaving a minor gap.
metrics: Spell must have an expiration date

assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism is mentioned; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop could apply, which is weak. There is no on-chain automatic check, capital at risk, or named penalty for this review step.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Copies Executive Template
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to copy the Executive Document template into the working branch for drafting.
assessments.quote: The template for the Executive Document is stored in the Executive Votes template directory ([https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/tree/main/templates](https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/tree/main/templates)) on GitHub. The Core Facilitator must copy the template into the working branch to draft the Executive Document.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule defines an exact actor (Core Facilitator), a specific action (copy the template), and the source URL in a verifiable way. A third party could check whether the template was copied into the working branch, but the text does not define 'working branch' explicitly, a minor gap.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism is mentioned; only the generic misalignment/adjudication processes (catch-all) would apply, which is always weak for this rule. No on-chain or named institutional mechanism directly covers this procedural step.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Creates Summary
assessments.description: Mandates specific disclosure requirements for executive proposals regarding office-hours, pause delays, and expiry terms.
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must create a summary that refers to every action included in the proposal. Under the Executive summary, the Core Facilitator must include the following details:

1. Office-Hours Modifier:
    - If the office-hours parameter has the value "Yes" and will be present in the Spell code, this must be explicitly mentioned:
        - "This Executive Proposal includes an office-hours modifier that means that it **can only be executed between 14:00 and 21:00 UTC, Monday - Friday**."
2. GSM Pause Delay:
    - The GSM Pause Delay period and affected items must be clearly communicated.
    - The term "GSM Pause Delay" must include a link to the Atlas document specifying its definition [A.1.10.3.1 - Pause Delay](3c9545d9-775f-4149-88bf-7d297b5302c6).
    - The current value of the GSM Pause Delay must include a link to the Atlas document specifying its value [A.1.10.3.1.2 - Pause Delay Current Value](db442d8a-8d98-47a2-b162-01c2adc22b67).
3. Proposal Expiry:
    - The expiry of the proposal must be explicitly noted, including the length of time for which the proposal is valid:
        - "If this Executive Proposal does not pass within 30 days, then it will expire and can no longer have any effect on the Sky Protocol."
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule specifies exact required language for the office‑hours case, mandatory links for GSM Pause Delay, and an unambiguous obligation to state the proposal expiry with its length. The requirement that the GSM Pause Delay period and affected items be 'clearly communicated' introduces a minor qualitative element, preventing a perfect 5.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Specifies Entities In Preamble
assessments.description: Mandates the specification of entities responsible for publishing votes and reviewing executive code.
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must specify the entities responsible for publishing the Executive Vote on the Voting Portal, as well as the Crafters and Reviewers of the executive code. The entities should be specified at the entity level.

- The publishers of the Executive Vote are the Core Facilitator.
- The Crafters and Reviewers alternate between Dewiz and Sidestream.
- The Crafters and Reviewers are determined during the GovOps meeting and recorded in the Executive Sheet.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule explicitly names actors (Core Facilitator, Dewiz, Sidestream), specifies an alternating pattern, and mandates recording in the Executive Sheet. A third party can verify compliance by checking the sheet, though no strict sequence start or deadline is given, a minor gap.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) covers this rule: Core GovOps reviews the Executive Sheet and related artifacts, and can penalize non-compliance, providing a specific enforcement path beyond the catch-all.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Includes Every Item From Executive Sheet
assessments.description: Mandates specific documentation and transparency requirements for the Core Facilitator when preparing Executive Documents.
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that every item from the Executive Sheet is included in the details section of the Executive Document. These items should be presented in order of judged impact/importance. If the order of items in the Executive Document differs from the Executive Sheet, the Executive Sheet must be updated to match, maintaining consistency between the two documents.

The Core Facilitator must make sure that each item:

- Includes links to the reasoning and authorization for its inclusion.
- Provides additional links required for voters to understand the context surrounding the item’s inclusion.
- Uses future-conditional language and clearly outlines the actions that will take place if the Executive Proposal passes. For example, phrasing such as "If this Executive Proposal passes, then this action will take place" ensures clarity and avoids ambiguity.
- Has hyperlinked key parameters, terms, and contracts where appropriate, making it easier for voters to access relevant information. Ethereum and IPFS addresses should also be linked to provide direct access to technical details.

The Core Facilitator must also make sure that the parties implicated in the proposal outcome are aware of the wording used for each item in the Executive Document.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule enumerates concrete steps (include all items, update sheet for consistency, list of required link types, future-conditional phrasing, hyperlinked addresses) but criteria like 'judged impact/importance', 'where appropriate', and 'required for voters to understand the context' are qualitative and not objectively measurable. No numeric thresholds or formulas are given.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The Agent Artifact Review by Core GovOps (d4bf73e7) can plausibly cover the Executive Document as an agent artifact; a violation could be identified during scheduled review and trigger penalty assessment, though no quantitative consequence is defined for this specific rule.

assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule defines a clear trigger (updates before handover), a specific communication channel (Slack thread), and the required recipients (Spell Team). However, it lacks any quantitative metrics, thresholds, or deadlines, making it a qualitative procedure.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism beyond the generic misalignment backstop (c6c6f595) reaches this notification rule. It is a simple process step with no specified penalty or oversight.

assessments.title: Ecosystem Spell Validation Window
assessments.description: Defines the mandatory time window for validating Spells between voting visibility and GSM Pause Delay expiration.
assessments.quote:
The Ecosystem Spell Validation Window is the period of time during which a Spell can be validated. Validation must occur:

1. After the Spell becomes visible and is available for voting on the Voting Portal (start of the validation window).
2. Before the Spell’s actions become executable, which occurs when the `GSM Pause Delay` elapses (end of the validation window).

Validation outside this window is ineffective because:

- The Spell may still be subject to changes before the start of the validation window.
- The Spell may already be executable after the end of the validation window.

The duration of the validation window is determined by the value of the GSM Pause Delay.

assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule states that validation outside the window is ineffective, which is a design consequence, but no specific enforcement mechanism (on-chain or otherwise) is cited in the text or reachable via known catalog mechanisms. The built-in ineffectiveness amounts to self-enforcement, which is always weak.

assessments.title: Ecosystem Spell Verification Scope
assessments.description: Defines the scope of code subject to Spell validation and identifies excluded instant actions.
assessments.quote:
The scope of Spell validation includes any code in the Sky Protocol that:

1. Must adhere to the `GSM Pause Delay` enforced by the Sky Protocol’s `ds-pause` contract, and
2. Is directly executed by the Sky Protocol’s `Pause Proxy` contract.

Actions that do not meet these criteria—such as `instant actions`, `MOM` and `IAM` contract calls—are excluded from Spell validation.

This exclusion is due to the absence of a pause delay for such actions, which prevents ecosystem actors from having sufficient time to perform their reviews.

Validators should also consider validating the source code or associated audits for contracts added to the Chainlog as part of a Spell, even if these contracts are not immediately executed or fall outside the standard validation scope. This includes pre-deployed emergency Spell contracts, ensuring that their integrity and security are assessed at the time of addition to the Chainlog for potential future use.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Ensure Tests Pass
assessments.description: Requires Ecosystem Spell validators to execute and pass all predefined GitHub repository tests for every Spell.
assessments.quote:
Ecosystem Spell validators must execute the predefined tests associated with a Spell. These tests are provided as scripts in the Spell repository on GitHub. Validators must run these scripts to verify the correctness, security, and compatibility of the Spell. All tests must pass successfully—without errors or failures—for the Spell to pass validation.

The best practice for running the tests are specified herein:

1. If you haven’t cloned the repository before, run: `git clone <https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/Spells-mainnet`>.
2. Navigate to the Spell repository directory by running: `cd Spells-mainnet`.
3. Update the repository for the latest changes by running: `git pull`.
4. Switch to the correct branch by finding the name from the Spell’s pull request on GitHub, run the command: `git checkout NAME`.
5. Verify your setup and check that you’re on the correct branch by running: `git status`.
6. Clean up old Spell library dependencies by running the command: `rm -r lib` or deleting the `lib` folder and its contents.
7. Install libraries required for the current Spell by running `git submodule update --init --recursive`.
8. Configure the local or remote node being used by running `export ETH_RPC_URL=URL` with the URL of your local or remote node. If using a remote node, do not share the URL as it can be used maliciously.
9. Run the Spell tests by running `make test`. If there are concerns about potential modifications to the function, validators can bypass the `make` command and directly execute the test script using `./scripts/test-dssSpell-forge.sh`.
10. Wait for completion. Allow 20 to 60 minutes for the tests to complete.
11. Review and Save Results: Save the test results (pass or fail) for logging purposes.

Alternatively, an online tool like diff checker ([https://www.diffchecker.com/](https://www.diffchecker.com/)) can be used. The Spell code on Etherscan should be compared with the `DssSpell.sol` in the GitHub repository for the relevant Spell. If the Spell goes live before the code is merged to the main branch, it’s possible to find the branch by the Target Date name of the Spell (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD).

When comparing, note that the following differences are acceptable and should not be flagged (based on validation guides):

- Comments: Lines starting with `//` or inside `/* */`.
- Imports and Solidity versions: Multiple declarations in the GitHub code.
- Interfaces: Numerical suffixes like `_1` or `_2` added to interface names in the contract.
- DssExecLib Interface: Extra code or warnings within the `DssExecLib` library.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Is Not A DarkSpell
assessments.description: Validators must verify Spells do not execute external contracts or use pre-defined addresses to prevent DarkSpells.
assessments.quote:
Validators must confirm that the deployed Spell does not execute an external `DssAction` contract. This validation ensures that the Spell is self-contained, does not rely on external contracts or pre-defined Ethereum addresses, and that the `DssExec` and `DssSpellAction` contracts are deployed together and not separately, as is done when using DarkSpells. Validators must perform the following two checks:

1. Check that the DssAction contract’s `execute()` function only calls the `actions()` function and does not interact with any external contracts or explicitly defined Ethereum addresses.
2. Check that the second argument used in the constructor when instantiating the `DssExec` is a newly created Spell action contract (e.g. `address(new DssSpellAction())`) and not an explicitly defined Ethereum address. This confirms that the Spell is linked to the correct action contract.

If either of these checks fails, the Spell cannot pass validation.

The validation checks can be performed by navigating to the "Contract tab" on Etherscan for the deployed Spell. In the source code, first locate the `DssAction` contract (or its equivalent, such as `DssSpellAction`). Review the `execute()` function and make sure that it only calls the `actions()` function. Then, locate the constructor and confirm that the `action` argument is instantiated as a new contract.

1. Using an Online Tool:

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Review Constants
assessments.description: Requires validators to verify rate precision units and call drip before implementing rate changes.
assessments.quote:
Validators should ensure that the rates are defined as per-second accumulation values, using the correct precision units common in the Sky Protocol (e.g., RAY for rates, RAD for debt/DAI amounts, WAD for general token amounts).

**Precision Units Overview**:

- **WAD (10^18)**: Used for token amounts and balances.
- **RAD (10^45)**: Used for debt values, ceilings, or large accumulations.
- **RAY (10^27)**: Used for rates and multipliers.

These units prevent floating-point issues in Solidity — always confirm they're applied correctly to avoid overflows or miscalculations. Group this with general constant validations (e.g., ensuring hardcoded values like fees or ceilings are computed accurately).

Rate values can be validated against the commented rate by using the `bc` command in a bash shell. Using the `NEW_FEE` variable in the example contract the following is visible: `bc -l <<< 'scale=27; e( l(1.095)/(60 * 60 * 24 * 365) )`. This produces 1.000000002877801985002875644. Removing the decimal place will allow you to see that this matches the definition of `NEW_FEE`.

Validating all rate adjustments can be done the same way. For more information on the rates module, refer to the developer guide ([https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/developerguides/blob/master/mcd/intro-rate-mechanism/intro-rate-mechanism.md](https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/developerguides/blob/master/mcd/intro-rate-mechanism/intro-rate-mechanism.md)). For easy reference, common pre-computed rates can also be viewed at the following ipfs link ([https://ipfs.io/ipfs/QmefQMseb3AiTapiAKKexdKHig8wroKuZbmLtPLv4u2YwW](https://ipfs.io/ipfs/QmefQMseb3AiTapiAKKexdKHig8wroKuZbmLtPLv4u2YwW)).

Immediately prior to making rate changes, `drip` must be called on the respective contracts.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Review Contract For Unusual Elements
assessments.description: Requires validators to perform specific code-level security checks on contracts during the spell validation process.
assessments.quote:
Validators should assess whether any unusual or unexpected elements appear in the contract. It could be:

- Hidden state changes: Look for retrieval functions (e.g., `get` or `view`) that include assignments (`=`), indicating state changes.
- External Calls At The End: Check for external calls (e.g., `.call`, `.send`, `.transfer`) made after state changes, as this could indicate potential reentrancy attacks.
- Force Ether, DAI or SKY Reception: Look for a `receive` function with no logic, which could forcibly receive assets.
- Use of `tx.origin`: The tx.origin variable refers to the address that started the current transaction. If `tx.origin` is used instead of `msg.sender` in decision-making processes, it could lead to unintended authorization.
- Function Naming Overlaps: A contract might have function names that are similar or overlap with common Solidity functions to mislead a reviewer. Check for misleading function names (e.g., `transfer`, `approve`, `mint`) with unexpected logic or assignments.

To perform this validation the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and review the source code.

assessments.quote:
Issues discovered during validation must be reported as follows:

1. Mandatory Reporting: If the validation check is required, the issue must be reported immediately.
2. Recommended Reporting: If the validation check is recommended, validators are strongly encouraged to report issues unless they are certain the issue is not malicious, a bug, or an attack on the Sky Protocol.
3. Out-of-Scope Issues: Any issues found outside the scope of validation checks should also be reported as soon as it is found.

In general, any issue that appears functional or potentially functional should be reported.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to report issues is clear, but entirely qualitative: no numeric thresholds, metrics, or defined deadlines exist; 'immediately' and 'as soon as it is found' are ambiguous, and what constitutes a reportable issue remains subjective. Compliance would be arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific consequence attaches to not reporting; only the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop (which is always weak) could theoretically be invoked, and no named penalty or automatic mechanism reaches this validator reporting duty.

assessments.title: Resolving Issues
assessments.description: Defines the validator's authority to resolve reported issues and prevents spell passing if issues remain unresolved.
assessments.quote:
When an issue has been reported by a Spell validator, the Core Facilitator or the Spell Team who worked on the Spell is likely to respond to the issue. The Spell validator must assume that the parties providing the answer are acting maliciously and lying to prevent the discovery of their attack.

The validator may only consider the issue as resolved once they are comfortable that the issue does not constitute a bug or attack that poses a threat to the Sky Protocol. Only the validator who raised the issue is permitted to consider an issue as resolved, and any unresolved issue will prevent the Spell from passing validation.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: No quantitative thresholds, deadlines, or objective verification criteria. The validator's obligation is expressed entirely in subjective language ('must assume malicious intent', 'comfortable that the issue does not constitute a bug or attack'), making compliance arguable based on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule defines a duty for the validator but contains no specific consequence for violation (e.g., resolving an issue without being truly comfortable). The only potential enforcement path is the generic misalignment/adjudication backstop, which is always weak. No named enforcement mechanism from the catalog or the paragraph text reaches this rule.

No on-chain, capital-at-risk, or named penalty path exists for a validator failing to report.

assessments.title: Outcome Of The Executive Proposal Vote
assessments.description: Defines the voting threshold requirements and the 30-day expiration period for official Spells.
assessments.quote: When an Executive Proposal is ready for a vote by Sky Governance, SKY holders cast their votes. The voting process determines whether the Executive Proposal gains enough support to move forward to the execution phase. If the executive does not accumulate sufficient SKY to "move the hat" (i.e., reach the required threshold for approval), it does not proceed to execution immediately; however, it can still gain support and be executed later within the expiration window. For official Spells, there is a 30-day expiration period after deployment. Once this period lapses, the Spell process ends, and no further actions can be taken for the associated Spell. If the executive gains enough support to be approved, the process moves forward to the execution phase.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule specifies a concrete 30‑day expiration deadline for official Spells but the voting approval threshold is described only qualitatively as 'sufficient SKY to move the hat' — no numeric value or formula is given, so a third party cannot verify compliance without external definition.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism is cited in the paragraph or identifiable in the catalog that ensures this rule is followed; expiration is a procedural deadline with only the generic misalignment backstop available.

To lift a Spell, that Spell must have more approvals than the current hat. This action is permissionless, meaning any Ethereum address can trigger the execution without requiring special permissions.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states an objective, on-chain verifiable condition: a Spell must have more approvals than the current hat. No ambiguous terms, a clear actor (any address), and the condition is fully quantifiable relative to the chain state.
metrics: more approvals than the current hat

After confirming hat status, the chief-keeper proceeds to schedule the Spell, ensuring that only the current hat is scheduled for execution.

assessments.title: Execution Setup For Approved Vote
assessments.description: Defines the permissionless scheduling process and required parameters for executing approved Spells via the ds-pause contract.
assessments.quote:
If the executive is approved and has been lifted to become the current hat in the DSChief, a future action to execute the Spell's actions is prepared by calling `schedule()` on the Spell contract. This action is permissionless, meaning any Ethereum address can trigger the execution without requiring special permissions. This process involves calling `plot` on `ds-pause` with four parameters related to the Spell action contract:

- The address of the Spell action contract.
- The `extcodehash` value of the Spell action contract.
- Any `calldata` information required for the future execution of the Spell contract's actions using `execute()`.
- The `eta`, which is the earliest time the Spell's actions can be executed. This must be scheduled at least the duration of the pause delay into the future.

Once the Spell's actions are "plotted" in the Pause, the Spell is considered `scheduled`, and the countdown to the `eta` time begins. In the absence of Office Hours, this countdown is typically equal to the duration of the `GSM Pause Delay`. If Office Hours are set to "Yes" then the countdown will be equal to the `GSM Pause Delay` plus whatever time is needed to enter the Office Hours window.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule specifies a clear condition for scheduling: the eta must be at least the pause delay duration into the future. This is a quantifiable threshold expressed in terms of a defined system parameter, but the value of the pause delay is not stated in this paragraph, requiring external lookup — a minor gap.
metrics: the eta must be scheduled at least the duration of the pause delay into the future
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism from the rubric's catalog applies; the on-chain enforcement by the ds-pause contract is not covered by a listed UUID, and no other consequence (penalties, conservatorship, etc.) is referenced for a violation of this scheduling rule. The catch-all misalignment process alone is weak.

assessments.title: Casting And Execution Of Approved Spell
assessments.description: Defines the atomic and permissionless execution process for Spells once the scheduled eta has passed.
assessments.quote: Once the current time exceeds the `eta` value set during scheduling, the Spell can be `cast` (see [A.1.10.2.4.13.3 - Execution Setup For Approved Vote](e06f6a83-7c74-4abd-b4da-771cbfdf2fb9)). Casting and the subsequent execution path occur atomically within the same transaction. This entire process is permissionless, meaning any Ethereum address can trigger the execution without requiring special permissions.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states a clear, objectively verifiable condition: once the current time exceeds the eta value set during scheduling, the Spell can be cast atomically and permissionlessly. The threshold (eta) is defined elsewhere but is a precise timestamp; the actor is any Ethereum address; compliance is checkable from the text alone.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: On-chain automatic enforcement: the Spell casting contract enforces the time > eta condition atomically; violation is impossible because the transaction reverts if eta not reached. This self-executing logic is defined in the referenced Execution Setup document (e06f6a83...), making the rule fully enforced by the contract code.

assessments.title: Casting Of Spell
assessments.description: Defines the execution sequence and state change for the DssSpell cast function.
assessments.quote:
When the `cast` function in the DssSpell contract is called:

- The Spell is marked as `cast`, preventing it from being executed again.
- The `cast` function initiates the execution process by calling the `exec` function in the `ds-pause` contract.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule enumerates concrete, verifiable steps (mark as cast, prevent re-execution, call exec) that define the DssSpell contract's behavior. Compliance is objectively checkable from the code, but no numeric threshold or metric is stated.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism from the catalog or the document text specifically reaches this rule; the on-chain behavior is self-enforcing, which the rubric treats as weak. Only the generic misalignment backstops (catch-all) could apply, which alone is always weak.

assessments.title: Execution Of Spell
assessments.description: Defines the step-by-step technical execution process for governance spells via the ds-pause and Pause Proxy contracts.
assessments.quote:
Within the same transaction initiated by `cast()`, ds-pause proceeds as follows:

1. Validation and Removal: The `exec` function in `ds-pause` validates the execution request and removes it from the list of scheduled executions.
2. Delegate Call to Spell Action Contract: The `ds-pause` contract calls `exec` on the Pause Proxy contract, which performs a `delegatecall` to the Spell action contract address specified during scheduling.
3. Execution of Spell Actions:
    - For regular Spells, the Pause Proxy calls the `execute()` function on the `DssSpellAction` contract.
    - The `execute()` function calls the `actions()` function, where the Spell’s actions are carried out.
4. Error Handling: If the transaction reverts at any point (e.g., due to an error in `actions()`), the Pause Proxy halts execution.
5. Final Checks: If the transaction succeeds, the `exec` function in `ds-pause` performs a final ownership check to ensure the Pause Proxy is still owned by `ds-pause`.
6. Completion: Once the final check passes, the execution of `cast()` is finalized, marking the end of the process.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph describes the on-chain technical process of spell execution via ds-pause, not an obligation for any regulated party; it is a procedural narration with no compliance requirement, no actor, no metric, and nothing to verify.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No rule is imposed, so no enforcement applies; any purely documentary description of an on-chain process cannot be linked to a named enforcement mechanism from the catalog, and the rule text itself contains no UUID. Hence, enforcement is weak.

assessments.title: Facilitator Updates Atlas To Reflect Spell Outcome

Following the successful execution of a Spell, the Atlas must be updated to accurately reflect the resulting changes. The Core Facilitator is responsible for ensuring that all relevant Sky Core Atlas documents are modified to incorporate the outcome of the Spell. For modifications pertaining to Agent Artifacts, the Operational Facilitator for the affected Agent is responsible for carrying out the required follow-up changes.

The updates must be completed in a timely manner following Spell execution, and must not introduce changes beyond those necessitated by the Spell outcome.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names specific actors (Core Facilitator, Operational Facilitator) and a clear action (updating Atlas documents), but the sole operative criterion 'timely manner' is qualitative, making compliance arguable.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Failure by an Operational Facilitator to update Agent Artifacts as required would be detected in the scheduled Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7), which includes penalty assessment, providing a defined path beyond the generic misalignment backstop. The Core Facilitator's analogous duty for non-artifact documents lacks a similarly citable mechanism, but the existence of an artifact-specific enforcement path yields a mid rating overall.

assessments.title: Continuous Approval Voting
assessments.description: Defines the Continuous Approval Voting mechanism and vote-weight limits for executive governance proposals.
assessments.quote:
Executive Votes operate under a Continuous Approval Voting mechanism. Voters can support multiple proposals by allocating their SKY vote-weight to each, with the goal of helping a favored proposal surpass the current "hat"—the proposal with the most approval in the DSChief contract. Voters can apply their full SKY vote-weight to up to 5 different proposals simultaneously (as defined by the `max_yays` limit in the contract), rather than splitting their tokens between them. If SKY token holders disagree with a new proposal, they can redirect their SKY vote-weight to the inactive proposal with the highest vote-weight (often the last successfully passed proposal) to maintain the status quo or support an alternative. An active proposal can become the hat if it accumulates more votes than any other, including the current hat, at which point it is "lifted" to become the new hat. This lifting process marks the active proposal, and it may now be scheduled and later executed, provided it meets other conditions like the GSM Pause Delay. There are three key aspects to Continuous Approval Voting:
- Victory threshold set by the hat: The vote-weight on the current hat proposal establishes the "victory threshold" that new proposals must exceed to become eligible for execution. This ensures only the most supported changes advance.
- Dynamic vote-weight movement: Vote-weight can shift from the hat to a new proposal, simultaneously lowering the victory threshold for the hat while boosting the new proposal's chances. This fluidity allows for real-time community consensus shifts.
- Securing the hat: Vote-weight is encouraged to remain on the hat proposal even after it's lifted, acting as a security measure against "rogue" or less-supported proposals that might attempt to overtake it with minimal backing.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule defines a voting mechanism with a numeric limit (max_yays=5) and an objectively verifiable threshold (vote-weight on the current hat). A third party can check compliance from the text alone.
metrics: victory threshold established by vote-weight on the current hat proposal
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism document from the catalog applies to this governance rule. While the contract itself enforces the mechanism, no UUID is available to meet the rubric's citation requirement; hence enforcement is rated weak.

assessments.title: Voting Outcome
assessments.description: Defines the SKY vote-weight threshold required for a proposal to pass and proceed to execution.
assessments.quote: The voting outcome is determined by the amount of SKY vote-weight allocated to the Executive Vote. If a proposal does not receive more SKY vote-weight than the current hat, it will not be scheduled for execution and will eventually expire; SKY holders can continue supporting it or redirect their vote-weight to another proposal, often the previously approved one, to maintain the status quo. For details of the execution process see [A.1.10.2.4.13 - Spell Execution Process And Retro (Step 13)](761cd866-17a9-47f5-8ae6-ab1788371be1).
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states a clear, objective condition: a proposal passes only if it receives more SKY vote-weight than the current hat. This is a binary, verifiable threshold that any third party can check.
metrics: more SKY vote-weight than the current hat
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule is automatically enforced by the governance contracts: the Spell Execution Process (referenced in the text) will not schedule a proposal for execution unless it becomes the hat, which requires satisfying this vote-weight condition. The enforcement is on-chain and deterministic.

assessments.title: Audit Process
assessments.description: Requires independent third-party security audits for smart contracts and deployment scripts before ecosystem deployment.
assessments.quote: The documents herein define the audit process for smart contracts and deployment scripts that require independent security review before inclusion in a Spell or deployment within the Sky Ecosystem. As part of this process, Sky Core engages independent third-party security firms to perform audits.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states that Sky Core engages third-party security firms for audits, but provides no quantified criteria, thresholds, cadence, or verification standards. Compliance is arguable based on the mere act of engagement, not the depth or frequency of audits.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific enforcement mechanism targets this rule. Only the generic misalignment backstop applies, which is insufficient for anything above weak.

assessments.title: Audit Triggers
assessments.description: Mandates audits for all new smart contract code and deployment scripts before ecosystem introduction.
assessments.quote:
An audit is required before new smart contract code is introduced to the Sky Ecosystem, including:

- Smart contracts and module onboardings
- Deployment and initialization scripts required to deploy and configure smart contracts, which must comply with the structure and requirements defined in [A.1.10.2.7.1.1 - Deployment And Initialization Script Standards](5f6012ba-450b-4620-baad-e602ee3e69f7)

This requirement does not extend to other code, such as off-chain services or user interfaces, unless separately specified.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule obligates an audit before code introduction but does not define audit scope, standards, or measurable criteria; compliance could be argued either way on the same facts (e.g., what constitutes a sufficient audit).
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The Agent Artifact Review process (d4bf73e7) includes scheduled reviews with penalty assessment; a Prime or Star that introduces unaudited code could be flagged and penalized via this mechanism, providing an institutional enforcement path with a distinct enforcer.

assessments.title: Deployment And Initialization Script Structure
assessments.description: Mandates specific library-based structures for contract deployment and initialization logic.
assessments.quote:
Deployment logic and initialization logic must be structured as follows:

- Deployment logic must be extracted into a Solidity library that accepts constructor arguments and deploys the contract.
- Initialization logic must be extracted into a Solidity library that performs post-deployment configuration, including granting roles and setting state.
- The deployment script must orchestrate the deployment by calling the deployment and initialization libraries.

Deployment and initialization logic must be combined into a single library unless there is reasonable justification for separation.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule specifies concrete steps (library extraction, script orchestration, single library unless justified) that can be verified in code, but the 'reasonable justification' exception is qualitative, leaving room for interpretation.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule is under audit triggers; violation would likely be caught during Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7), which can assess penalties, though the consequence is unquantified for this specific rule.

assessments.title: General Requirements
assessments.description: Mandates parameterization of addresses and 100% test coverage for all deployment and initialization library functions.
assessments.quote:
The following requirements apply to all deployment and initialization scripts:

- Libraries must not contain hardcoded addresses. All addresses and configuration values must be passed as parameters.
- All library functions must be tested. Test coverage must target 100%. Exceptions to this requirement must have reasonable justification.

Deployment verification, including confirmation of address correctness and on-chain state, is not within the scope of an audit of deployment and initialization scripts and must be performed as a separate deployment verification review.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule specifies a numeric threshold ('target 100% test coverage for all library functions') and a clear absolute prohibition on hardcoded addresses. However, the exception clause 'reasonable justification' introduces qualitative judgment, and the regulated actor is not explicitly named, leaving minor gaps.
metrics: Test coverage must target 100% for all library functions
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Compliance can be assessed via Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7), which examines security practices and can impose penalties, and the risk-based insurance pricing (fd1f682c) indirectly incentivizes adherence, though no quantified or on-chain penalty is specified for this rule.

assessments.title: Deployment Script Requirements
assessments.description: Requires deployment scripts to transfer ownership to governance and undergo mandatory audit verification.
assessments.quote:
Deployment scripts must satisfy the following requirements:

- Deployment scripts must yield ownership of deployed contracts to the relevant Governance proxy. Exceptions to this requirement must have reasonable justification.
- Top-level deployment scripts must be included in the audit scope. Auditors must at minimum verify constructor parameters.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states concrete obligations (transfer ownership, include in audit scope) but uses a qualitative exception ('reasonable justification') with no defined criteria, and provides no numeric thresholds, deadlines, or verifiable metrics.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The Agent Artifact Review By Core GovOps (d4bf73e7) mechanism includes scheduled review of agent artifacts, with penalty assessment for non-compliance. Deployment scripts would be captured under that review process, enabling enforcement, though the specific consequence for this rule is unquantified.

assessments.title: Initialization Script Requirements
assessments.description: Mandates that initialization libraries be importable by Spells and requires audits for all initialization functions.
assessments.quote:
Initialization scripts must satisfy the following requirements:

- The initialization library must be directly importable by a compliant Spell without modifications. The execution context of the library is expected to be the relevant Governance proxy.
- Every initialization function must be audited.
- Top-level initialization scripts that exist solely for test environments must not be included in the audit scope.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states three specific requirements: importability without modifications by a compliant Spell, auditing of all init functions, and exclusion of test-only top-level scripts from audit scope. These are clear binary conditions verifiable through inspection but no quantifiable thresholds.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Non-compliance with audit requirements constitutes poor security practice; the risk-based pricing of insurance mechanism (fd1f682c) would likely increase insurance fees for the responsible Prime, providing a priced incentive.

assessments.title: Audit Request And Intake
assessments.description: Defines the mandatory contents and submission process for code audit intake forms.
assessments.quote:
The team responsible for the code to be audited fills in a standardized audit intake form containing, at minimum:

- The scope of the audit, identifying the specific contracts, scripts, or artifacts to be reviewed
- The repository URL and exact commit hash of the code to be audited, which must have been reviewed as specified in [A.1.10.2.7.2.1 - Code Review Requirement](4bead31b-adee-4121-a966-d0e1c31f91e2)
- Any context the auditor needs to understand the purpose and integration of the audited code within the Sky Ecosystem

Core GovOps compiles the completed intake forms and submits them to the auditor. The audit request must be submitted with sufficient lead time for the auditor to complete the review before the target Spell or deployment date.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule imposes a clear obligation to complete an intake form with listed content items, but the lead time requirement ('sufficient') is a qualitative judgment, and no numeric thresholds, formulas, or objectively verifiable criteria are given. A third party could argue either way about compliance on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No specific consequence or enforcement mechanism is attached; only the generic misalignment backstop would theoretically apply, which alone is always weak.

assessments.quote: The commit hash submitted for audit must correspond to a Pull Request that has been reviewed and approved by at least one (1) member of the team responsible for the code who is not an author of the Pull Request. Evidence of the review and approval must be available to Core GovOps as part of the audit request and intake process specified in [A.1.10.2.7.2 - Audit Request And Intake](fcc17c4e-b1cd-4e62-bb2b-0aea02ee72d5).
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule sets a numeric threshold (at least one non-author reviewer) and a verifiable condition (the PR must have been reviewed and approved), enabling objective compliance checking. The evidence requirement, while not fully detailed, is tied to a specified intake process.

assessments.title: Audit Execution And Report Delivery
assessments.description: Defines mandatory contents and hosting requirements for interim and final audit reports.
assessments.quote:
The auditor performs the audit against the scope and commit hash specified in the audit request. Upon completion, the auditor delivers an interim audit report containing, at minimum:

- A scope statement identifying the contracts, scripts, or artifacts reviewed
- The exact commit hash of the audited code
- All findings, categorized by severity
- Recommendations for remediation where applicable

The final audit report must be hosted on the auditor's website or another independently verifiable location. Internal documents, shared drives, or non-permanent links do not satisfy this requirement.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule enumerates four concrete contents for the interim audit report, each verifiable (scope statement exists, commit hash is present, findings are listed with severity, recommendations included). The final report hosting requirement is unambiguous. Minor gaps: no delivery deadline defined beyond 'upon completion', and severity levels are referenced but not defined here.
